extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of humor theory, linguists, and researchers studying joke structure and generation (including computational humorists)
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and representational framework for analyzing and modeling jokes using script oppositions, logical mechanisms, and six knowledge resources; includes principles for ordering those resources into a hierarchy and necessary components for situational joke production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter 6: Script Opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The text of a joke is always fully or in part compatible with two distinct scripts and the two scripts are opposed to each other in a special way; the punchline triggers a switch from one script to the other by causing the hearer to backtrack and realize an alternate interpretation was possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Script oppositions operate at levels of abstraction: (most abstract) real vs. unreal, which can take forms actual vs. nonactual, normal vs. abnormal, possible vs. impossible; (lower-level) oppositions manifest as good vs. bad, life vs. death, sex vs. nonsex, money vs. no-money, high vs. low stature, etc. The nonactual script typically requires pseudological justification; trigger types (SSTH) include ambiguous and contradictory triggers that implement the script-switch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-level joke representation model
rubrics_metrics.description: A hierarchical model with five levels: Level 5 (Basic): script oppositions and logical mechanisms; Level 4 (Template): combines script opposition + logical mechanism; Level 3 (Target & Situation): selects target and situation; Level 2 (Language): assigns specific language form to the representation; Level 1 (Surface): the actual text of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each level represents different abstraction/operation: Level 5 contains abstract content (SO, LM), Level 4 operationally combines them into a template, Level 3 selects cultural instantiation (target, situation), Level 2 maps to linguistic choices (words, syntax), Level 1 is the resulting text. The model has theoretical issues (e.g., ordering of LM vs SO) discussed in the text and may be revised (some proposals collapse or reorder levels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Knowledge Resources (KRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are informed by six bodies of knowledge (KR): script oppositions (SO), logical mechanisms (LM), situations (SI), target (TA), narrative strategy (NS), and language (LA). Each KR is a list/set of options from which choices are made to produce or interpret a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each KR as a database of possible values; production/analysis of a joke involves selecting values from these KRs. The six KRs are the primary dimensions for characterizing, comparing, and generating jokes in the proposed theory (GTVH).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle L (Roseanne Barr rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If KR-X choices limit the choices within KR-Y, then X precedes Y in the hierarchy: 'the wider you are, the higher up you go.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized as a funnel metaphor: higher-level KRs have a wider array of choices that progressively narrow lower-level choices. Formal representation: choices in KR-X map to (reduce) allowed choices in KR-Y; thus top-down narrowing orders abstraction levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 2 (Donald Trump rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If KR-Y rigidly determines KR-X (i.e., each choice in Y uniquely determines X), then KR-Y should follow and not precede KR-X; otherwise the higher KR would absorb the lower, impoverishing the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigid determination implies subsumption (absorption) and should be avoided to keep distinct KRs meaningful. If rigid determination exists, merge or reorder the KRs so that determinative KRs follow determined ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (LA) as lowest/implementational KR
rubrics_metrics.description: The text of the joke (LA choices) implements, embodies, and reveals the choices made in the other five KRs; therefore LA should emerge after the other KRs and be placed lowest (closest to surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the punchline/text is fixed, variability in other KRs is limited; conversely, assuming LA choices made first precludes meaningful choice in other KRs. This yields the partial ordering KR* > LA in the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric relations among KRs (I/S/C/D distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pairwise relations among KRs can be Independence (I), Stylistic preference (S), Constraint (C), or rigid Determination (D); these relations inform partial ordering of KRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the paper: SO and LM are largely independent (I) though may show preferences; TA rigidly determines SO (D) in many cases because a target brings its stereotype; LM may constrain SI (C) and vice versa; NS may constrain LA but not affect SO/LM/SI/TA. Use I/S/C/D matrix to derive ordering and dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial ordering derived from binary relations
rubrics_metrics.description: From the asymmetrical relations among the six KRs the following partial orderings are inferred: KR* > LA; KR*(but LA) > NS; SO > TA (i.e., many KRs are higher/more abstract than language; script oppositions rank above target).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These orderings appear in a partial hierarchy (Figure 8) and are used to build a more complete hierarchy when combined with content/tool distinctions and similarity evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content vs Tool KR distinction (and modification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible dichotomy: content-oriented KRs = SO, TA, SI; tool-oriented KRs = LM, NS, LA. Modified proposal: LM primarily serves SO, while NS and LA serve multiple KRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This content/tool view can be used to motivate ordering (content higher, tools lower), but authors caution that simplistic dichotomy is imperfect and propose a modified assignment where LM is mainly a tool for SO and LA/NS are tools for multiple content KRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity-based ordering principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees of perceived similarity among jokes (based on differing KR choices) provide empirical anchoring for ordering KRs: fewer different KR choices → higher similarity → those KRs are lower-level (less abstract).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological guidance: use similarity judgments among exemplars (e.g., jokes (1)-(7)) to infer which KRs are more abstract; expect one-difference pairs to be more similar than two-difference pairs. Authors note psychological data may be noisy/borderline but can still inform hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSTH necessary components for situational (produced) jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: For situational joke production SSTH (Raskin 1985) lists required components: (i) a switch from bona-fide to non-bona-fide mode; (ii) the text of an intended joke; (iii) two (partially) overlapping scripts compatible with the text; (iv) an oppositeness relation between the two scripts; (v) a trigger realizing the oppositeness relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Component (i) is a precondition; (ii) includes the punchline; (iii)-(iv) pertain to script oppositions; (v) may be explicit or implied (puns are a frequent cheap trigger). These are practical diagnostic/production criteria for identifying or constructing situational jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target (TA) constraints and optionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Target selection often constrains or rigidly determines other KRs: TA rigidly determines SO when a group carries a dominant stereotype (e.g., Poles→dumb stereotype); TA also constrains SI and LA and may imply stylistic preferences for NS. TA is marked as an optional parameter in the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for analysis/creation: when choosing a target, consider cultural stereotypes and ensure compatibility with chosen script opposition and situation; avoid ambiguous targets that map to multiple stereotypes as this can confuse the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Mechanisms (LM) constraints and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: LM (e.g., figure-ground reversal, false analogy) is largely independent from SO but can show preferences; LM may constrain SI (a situation must afford the mechanism) and has stylistic preferences toward NS and LA, but LM does not generally constrain TA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling or constructing a joke, ensure the situation supports the chosen logical mechanism (e.g., figure-ground reversal requires a clear figure/ground); LM can be combined with different SOs and vice versa, though some pairings are more natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Strategy (NS) and Language (LA) tool relations
rubrics_metrics.description: NS may constrain some LA choices but does not affect SO, LM, SI, or TA; LA, however, can rigidly determine SO, LM, SI, TA, and NS because language choices instantiate and sometimes force particular readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: narrative form (riddle, expository, etc.) influences phrasing but typically not script/logic; but once language is fixed, it can lock in scripts and mechanisms, so careful LA design is crucial for intended script activation and trigger effectiveness.
